title: Have To and Must for Obligation
summary: Learn how to talk about rules and things you need to do. Discover the small difference between have to and must.

sections.p: We use have to when something is a rule. Another person or a law makes this rule for you. For example, your boss or a school makes the rule. You change the form for he, she, and it to has to. In negative sentences, we use don't have to or doesn't have to.

ex.en: I have to work on Monday.
ex.mean: My job requires me to work.

ex.en: She has to wear a uniform.

sections.p: We use must when the speaker thinks something is very important. It often comes from your own feelings, not an outside rule. Must is the same for all pronouns like I, you, he, and she. The negative form is mustn't, which means it is very important that you do not do something.

ex.en: I must call my mother today.
ex.mean: I really want to do this.
It is very important to be on time.

sections.p: Often, native speakers use have to and must in similar ways in everyday life. However, remember that have to often shows a general rule from the outside world. Must often shows a strong personal feeling or a strict rule written on a sign.

ex.en: I have to clean my room.
ex.mean: My parents want me to do it.
I feel it is very dirty and I want to clean it.

sections.p: We often make questions about rules using have to. We use do and does to ask questions in the present tense. We do not usually use must in questions for everyday rules.

ex.en: Do you have to work tomorrow?
ex.mean: Is it a work day for you?

ex.en: What time does she have to leave?
ex.mean: When is her required departure time?

tip: Remember that mustn't means 'do not do it', but don't have to means 'you have a choice'.

quiz.en: I ___ finish this report today. My boss said it is urgent.
Tomorrow is Saturday, so I ___ get up early.
She ___ wear a coat. It is very cold outside.
You ___ touch that wire! It is dangerous.
___ you have to work on weekends?
This food is delicious. You ___ try it!
